newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stays above battle in campaign finale.
newsitem.headline: Clinton stays above battle in campaign finale.

text.p: Clearly confident of victory in the Nov. 5 election, President Bill Clinton on Thursday focused on carrying Arizona, a feat no Democratic presidential candidate has managed since Harry Truman pulled it off in 1948.

Clinton's visit, for a campaign rally at Arizona State University, was a luxury he could ill afford unless he were sure of victory next Tuesday because the state offers just eight of the 270 electoral votes he needs to turn back a challenge from Republican Bob Dole and independent Ross Perot.

With most pre-election polls indicating that he leads Dole nationally by 12 to 17 percentage points, Clinton later was to campaign in Nevada -- another state normally hostile to Democrats -- before going on to California to try to strengthen his grip on its 54 electoral votes.

Clinton, revelling in his frontrunner status, plans to criss-cross the country between now and next Tuesday making a final appeal for votes. He began his sprint to the campaign finish line in Ypsilanti, Mich. on Wednesday and later went on to a rally in Denver, Colo.
"Bye Bye, folks. See you on Tuesday," he called to some Dole backers when they were ushered from the rally after staging a brief demonstration.

Aides said Clinton planned a major address in California on Friday on the issue of campaign finance reform, which has come to the fore in the last few weeks due to a welter of charges and counter-charges about Democratic and Republican political fundraising tactics.

Clinton has been ignoring Dole's efforts to bait him into a fight on the issue, and on Wednesday night he rejected Perot's challenge to an election eve debate on campaign finance and other ethics questions.

"The president has set his schedule for the balance of the campaign. We've identified the issues that we'll be addressing, including campaign finance. I think we'll be doing our events, not Mr. Perot's," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.

Clinton has endorsed a campaign finance reform proposal sponsored by Senators John McCain, an Arizona Republican, and Russell Feingold, a Democrat from Wisconsin, that would among other things outlaw "soft money" contributions -- big gifts to political parties to get around limits on giving to individual candidates.
Dole's Republicans used parliamentary tactics to kill the proposal in the Senate earlier this year.
